QMSBR—*Quantitative Methods for Social and Behavioral Research*—is a modular
collection of chapters designed to support more than one quantitative-methods
course. Reproducible computing resources may join later releases after separate
review. The collection is maintained as one canonical library so a correction
can improve every course route that uses it.

## The framework {#the-framework}

The **Argument-Based Framework for Quantitative Research** organizes the work
needed to answer a quantitative question in empirical research. The quantitative
question sits at the centre and is the organizing unit. An optional, preferably
prespecified hypothesis is a candidate answer; the final answer is a bounded
substantive claim whose strength and scope reflect the evidence, design,
assumptions, uncertainty, context, and reservations.

The framework distinguishes two linked four-part arguments:

| Statistical argument | Governing question |
|---|---|
| **STAT-E · Empirical evidence** | What data and data-production information were recorded for which units? |
| **STAT-J · Statistical justification** | Why can those records and the planned or fitted procedure address the estimand or predictive target, under which conditions? |
| **STAT-I · Statistical inference** | What estimand, estimate, uncertainty, checking, sensitivity, multiplicity, and analytic status connect the evidence to a claim? |
| **STAT-C · Bounded statistical claim** | What qualified statement is justified, with which statistical reservations? |

Within each argument, Evidence and Justification jointly support Inference,
which supports a bounded Claim. Across the two arguments, each substantive
component develops its statistical counterpart: SUB-E situates STAT-E, SUB-J
augments and evaluates STAT-J, SUB-I interprets STAT-I, and STAT-C bounds and
calibrates SUB-C.

| Substantive argument | Governing question |
|---|---|
| **SUB-E · Contextualized empirical evidence** | What do the cases, variables, and design information in STAT-E represent in their substantive population, setting, and period? |
| **SUB-J · Substantive justification** | Why does this contextualized evidence bear on the substantive question, claim type, and scope? |
| **SUB-I · Substantive inference and interpretation** | What does the result mean in substantive units and context, how important is it, and what alternatives remain? |
| **SUB-C · Bounded substantive claim (bounded answer)** | What final bounded answer is justified, including reservations and limits on causal or population generalization? |

The same framework has three coordinated perspectives: **Argument** asks what
must logically justify the answer; **Workflow** asks how the argument is built
and revised across eight iterative proposal and implementation stages; and
**Evaluation** uses seven named lenses---Question alignment, Evidence integrity,
Justification adequacy, Inferential adequacy, Transition fidelity, Claim
calibration, and Cross-question coherence. Multiple questions may share evidence
and support, but each requires a distinct traceable argument and answer outcome.

The framework is **Toulmin-informed**: it retains the need for evidence, a
justified inferential bridge, qualified claims, and explicit reservations without
treating the eight components as one-to-one replacements for Toulmin's six roles.
LeMire (2010) provides a related statistical precedent focused on
null-hypothesis testing. Chapter 1's Section 6, **How the Regression-Based
Approach Develops and Instantiates the Framework**, explains how regression
develops the available targets, comparisons, models, checks, and interpretive
obligations, and how a particular regression analysis instantiates all eight
components. Its Chapters 2--14 map is a subordinate guide to that development.

## Scope

Part One focuses mainly on observable variables, foundational statistical
reasoning, R, and regression. Factor analysis and latent-variable modelling are
reserved for Part Two; multilevel and longitudinal models are reserved for Part
Three. Study design is addressed wherever it controls interpretation, but
regression alone never creates a causal claim.

## Citation {#citation}

Please cite the release you used. Repository metadata are provided in
[CITATION.cff](../CITATION.cff); a suggested collection-level citation is:

> Chen, J. (2026). *QMSBR: Quantitative Methods for Social and Behavioral
> Research* (Version 2026.1).

Also cite the original datasets, software, and studies used by an analysis.

## Accessibility

HTML is the preferred reading format: it provides responsive layout, headings,
search, link text, and selectable code. Downloadable PDFs are retained for
printing and annotation and are checked for reading order, document language,
bookmarks, metadata, and visual integrity. Accessibility problems can be
reported through the repository issue tracker or by email.
